specStatements.text: The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time:
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken)
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken)
The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s.
For the Higher Tier, students are also required to use quantity of reactants in terms of moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s.
Students should be able to:
calculate the mean rate of a reaction from given information about the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of a product formed and the time taken
draw, and interpret, graphs showing the quantity of product formed or quantity of reactant used up against time
draw tangents to the curves on these graphs and use the slope of the tangent as a measure of the rate of reaction
(HT only) calculate the gradient of a tangent to the curve on these graphs as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.

Factors which affect the rates of chemical reactions include: the concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
Students should be able to recall how changing these factors affects the rate of chemical reactions.

Required practical 5: investigate how changes in concentration affect the rates of reactions by a method involving measuring the volume of a gas produced and a method involving a change in colour or turbidity.
This should be an investigation involving developing a hypothesis.

Collision theory explains how various factors affect rates of reactions. According to this theory, chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy. The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react is called the activation energy.

Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, and the surface area of solid reactants increases the frequency of collisions and so increases the rate of reaction.
Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.
Students should be able to :
predict and explain using collision theory the effects of changing conditions of concentration, pressure and temperature on the rate of a reaction
predict and explain the effects of changes in the size of pieces of a reacting solid in terms of surface area to volume ratio
use simple ideas about proportionality when using collision theory to explain the effect of a factor on the rate of a reaction.
Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.
A reaction profile for a catalysed reaction can be drawn in the following form:
Students should be able to identify catalysts in reactions from their effect on the rate of reaction and because they are not included in the chemical equation for the reaction.
Students should be able to explain catalytic action in terms of activation energy.
Students do not need to know the names of catalysts other than those specified in the subject content.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of catalysts other than those specified in the subject content.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No item asks a student to recall the name of a catalyst. Where a substance is named it is supplied in the stem as data (the solid in q28 is left unnamed and identified only from its effect on the rate and its absence from the equation 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂). Enzymes are named only because the specification itself names them as the catalysts of biological systems. No item requires catalyst names for industrial processes, transition-metal catalyst names, or any catalyst met elsewhere in the course, and no distractor punishes a student for not knowing one.

scopeNotes.statement: For the Higher Tier, students are also required to use quantity of reactants in terms of moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s. (HT only) calculate the gradient of a tangent to the curve on these graphs as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two requirements the specification restricts to the Higher Tier are kept inside items tagged tier "higher" and nowhere else. Moles as a quantity and mol/s as a unit of rate appear only in c06, m07, m08 and questions q06 and q07, all tagged tier "higher"; c03, c04 and m06 name moles only to flag that they are a Higher Tier extension. Numerical calculation of the gradient of a tangent appears only in c09, m15 and q13. Foundation-accessible items use mass in grams and volume in cm³ only, and ask only for a tangent to be drawn and its slope used as a measure of rate (q12), which is required of both tiers. The tier recorded in the input file for these statements is copied verbatim into specStatements; the derived items are tagged "higher" because the statements' own wording restricts them to that tier.

concepts.definition: How quickly a reaction proceeds. It can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time.
The average rate over a period of time: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken), or (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).
How much of a starting substance has been consumed in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
How much of a new substance has been made in a given time, measured as a mass in grams or as a volume in cm³ (moles at Higher Tier).
The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s, because a quantity is divided by a time.
At Higher Tier the quantity of reactants may be given in moles, and the rate of reaction is then given in mol/s.
A graph of the quantity of product formed, or of reactant used up, plotted against time. Its steepness at any point shows how fast the reaction is going.
A straight line drawn so that it just touches a curve at one point. Its slope is used as a measure of the rate of reaction at that moment.
The change in the y quantity divided by the change in time along the tangent, calculated as a measure of rate of reaction at a specific time.
The concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
The amount of a dissolved substance in a given volume of solution. A more concentrated solution has more reactant particles in the same volume.
How tightly gas particles are packed. Raising the pressure of reacting gases puts more particles into the same volume.
The area of solid exposed to the other reactant. Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes more of it.
The cloudiness of a mixture. A reaction that makes an insoluble solid grows cloudy, and the time for a mark to disappear can be timed.
A testable prediction about how one variable will affect another, which the investigation is then designed to test.
Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
How many collisions happen each second. Increasing it increases the rate of reaction.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
The surface area of a solid divided by its volume. Smaller pieces of the same mass have a larger surface area to volume ratio.
A simple idea used with collision theory: doubling the number of particles in a given volume roughly doubles the collision frequency, and so roughly doubles the rate.
A substance that changes the rate of a chemical reaction but is not used up during the reaction. Different reactions need different catalysts.
A biological catalyst. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
The route a reaction takes from reactants to products. A catalyst provides a different pathway that has a lower activation energy.
An energy diagram for a reaction. For a catalysed reaction it is drawn with a lower hump, while the reactants and products stay at the same energies.

misconceptions.question: Reaction A finishes in 20 s, reaction B in 200 s, and both make the same amount of gas. Which has the greater rate?
misconceptions.correct: Reaction A: the same quantity of gas in a shorter time is a faster reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Reaction B is faster because 200 is a bigger number of seconds than 20.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Time is the number the student actually measured, so it feels like the answer, and in everyday speech 'a long reaction' sounds like 'a big reaction'.
misconceptions.correction: Time is the denominator, not the rate. Mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken), so a longer time gives a smaller rate for the same quantity.

misconceptions.question: Is the total volume of gas given off enough on its own to give the rate of a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No: a time is needed as well, because rate is a quantity divided by a time.
misconceptions.misconception: The total volume of gas collected is the rate of the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'How much gas did it make?' and 'how fast did it make it?' both feel like measures of how well the reaction went.
misconceptions.correction: The rate of a chemical reaction is found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time. A quantity on its own is not a rate.

misconceptions.question: 3.6 g of magnesium is used up in 180 s. What is the mean rate?
misconceptions.correct: 0.020 g/s, from 3.6 g divided by 180 s.
misconceptions.misconception: 50 g/s, from 180 s divided by 3.6 g.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that a division is needed but not which way round, and dividing the big number by the small one gives a tidier answer.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity always goes on top: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken).

misconceptions.question: A rate is worked out as 0.6. How should it be written?
misconceptions.correct: 0.6 cm³ /s, because a rate is a quantity per second.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.6 cm³ , because that is the unit of the quantity that was measured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The unit is copied from the measuring cylinder or balance and the 'per second' part of the calculation is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s: the time unit must appear.

misconceptions.question: How does the specification say the quantity of reactant or product may be measured?
misconceptions.correct: By the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .
misconceptions.misconception: By the concentration in mol/dm³ or by the temperature in °C.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Concentration and temperature are the quantities most often written on the bottles and read off in rate experiments, so they feel like the measured quantity.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ . Temperature is a condition, not a quantity of substance.

misconceptions.question: Gas volume in cm³ is collected each second. What is the unit of rate?
misconceptions.correct: cm³ /s.
misconceptions.misconception: s/cm³ , written with the time on top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The unit is assembled from the words in the order they were spoken ('seconds per centimetre cubed') rather than from the division that was done.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity divided by the time gives the quantity on top: g/s or cm³ /s, and mol/s at Higher Tier.

misconceptions.question: A Higher Tier question gives the reactant in moles. What is the unit of rate?
misconceptions.correct: mol/s.
misconceptions.misconception: mol/dm³ , because that is the unit that goes with moles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: mol/dm³ is the unit met most often with moles, in concentration work, so it is recalled first.
misconceptions.correction: For the Higher Tier, quantity of reactants may be in moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s. mol/dm³ is a concentration, not a rate.

misconceptions.question: 0.060 mol of hydrogen forms in 30 s. What is the mean rate?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0020 mol/s, from 0.060 divided by 30.
misconceptions.misconception: 1.8 mol/s, from 0.060 multiplied by 30.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Multiplying is the safer-feeling operation when the numbers are awkward, and it avoids a small decimal answer.
misconceptions.correction: Rate is a division: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).

misconceptions.question: A flask loses 0.60 g of mass in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0050 g/s, from 0.60 g divided by 120 s.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.60 g/s, because 0.60 g is what the reaction lost.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mass loss is the number the student worked out first, so it is reported as the answer with a rate unit stuck on the end.
misconceptions.correction: The mass lost is the quantity of reactant used. It must still be divided by the time taken to give a rate.

misconceptions.question: Experiment X makes 30 cm³ in 20 s; experiment Y makes 45 cm³ in 45 s. Which is faster?
misconceptions.correct: X, at 1.5 cm³ /s against 1.0 cm³ /s for Y.
misconceptions.misconception: Y, because it produced the larger total volume of gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The bigger number of cm³ is the more obvious comparison, and the times are not brought into it.
misconceptions.correction: Rates must be compared after dividing each quantity by its own time taken.

misconceptions.question: A gas-volume curve is steep at first and then flattens. What does that show?
misconceptions.correct: The reaction is fastest at the start and slows down as reactants are used up.
misconceptions.misconception: The volume of gas is falling once the curve stops being steep.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A curve bending over is read as a curve going down, especially when it is described as 'levelling off'.
misconceptions.correction: The line still rises, just more slowly, so gas is still being made but at a lower rate.

misconceptions.question: The line on a gas-volume graph becomes horizontal after 80 s. What does that mean?
misconceptions.correct: No more gas is being made, so the reaction has finished.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas is now being produced at a steady, constant rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Straight line' is remembered as 'constant rate' from other graphs, without checking that this straight line has zero slope.
misconceptions.correction: A horizontal line has a gradient of zero, so the rate is zero and no more product is forming.

misconceptions.question: How is the rate at 30 s found from a curved graph?
misconceptions.correct: By drawing a tangent to the curve at 30 s and using its slope.
misconceptions.misconception: By reading the volume of gas off the curve at 30 s.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The graph gives a value at 30 s easily, and a reading feels like an answer while a slope feels like extra work.
misconceptions.correction: The height of the curve is the quantity so far. The rate is the slope of the tangent at that point.

misconceptions.question: A student joins the origin to the point at 30 s and calls the slope the rate at 30 s. Is that right?
misconceptions.correct: No: that gives the mean rate over the first 30 s, not the rate at 30 s.
misconceptions.misconception: The line from the origin to the point gives the rate at that moment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both lines are straight and both have a slope, so the difference between an average over a period and a value at an instant is missed.
misconceptions.correction: A tangent touches the curve at the point and matches its steepness there, which is why the specification asks for a tangent.

misconceptions.question: A tangent rises 40 cm³ while time goes from 10 s to 30 s. What is the rate?
misconceptions.correct: 2.0 cm³ /s, from 40 cm³ divided by 20 s.
misconceptions.misconception: 40 cm³ /s, using the rise on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The vertical change is the number that stands out on the graph, and the horizontal change is not read off.
misconceptions.correction: The gradient of a tangent is the change in quantity divided by the change in time.

misconceptions.question: Is the time a reaction is left for one of the factors that affect its rate?
misconceptions.correct: No: the listed factors are concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts.
misconceptions.misconception: Leaving a reaction for longer is a factor that makes it go faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Longer experiments give more product, so time is confused with a factor that changes the rate itself.
misconceptions.correction: Time changes how much product has formed, not how fast it forms. The specification lists concentration, pressure of reacting gases, surface area, temperature and catalysts.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the rate when a reaction mixture is cooled?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases, because collisions are less frequent and less energetic.
misconceptions.misconception: It increases, because cooling packs the particles closer together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cooling is linked to contraction and to particles slowing and settling, which is then read as particles being closer and so colliding more.
misconceptions.correction: Lowering the temperature lowers both the frequency and the energy of collisions, so the rate falls.

misconceptions.question: Does changing the temperature change the rate of a reaction, or only the amount of product?
misconceptions.correct: It changes the rate: higher temperature means a faster reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature only affects how much product is made, not how quickly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Yield and rate are both described as 'how well the reaction went', and the two are not separated.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to recall how changing temperature affects the rate of chemical reactions: raising it increases the rate.

misconceptions.question: Which two methods does Required practical 5 use to follow a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Measuring the volume of a gas produced, and a method involving a change in colour or turbidity.
misconceptions.misconception: Measuring the temperature rise of the mixture in the flask.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thermometers are used so often in practical chemistry that a temperature measurement is assumed to be part of any rate experiment.
misconceptions.correction: Required practical 5 uses a method involving measuring the volume of a gas produced and a method involving a change in colour or turbidity.

misconceptions.question: Which of these is a hypothesis: 'measure the gas every 10 s' or 'the higher the concentration, the faster the gas forms'?
misconceptions.correct: The second one: it predicts how one variable will affect another, so it can be tested.
misconceptions.misconception: A hypothesis is the list of steps you will carry out in the experiment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The method is the part of a write-up that is planned first and takes the most effort, so it is remembered as the important statement.
misconceptions.correction: A hypothesis is a testable prediction made before the results are collected; the steps are the method and the summary of the results is the conclusion.

misconceptions.question: Do all collisions between reacting particles cause a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No: only collisions with at least the activation energy lead to a reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Every collision between the reacting particles causes a reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Collision theory is remembered as 'particles must collide' and the energy condition attached to it is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

misconceptions.question: What is the activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy given out by the particles when they collide and react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy changes in reactions are met as energy released, so any energy quantity in a reaction is assumed to be energy given out.
misconceptions.correction: Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is a requirement to be met, not an output.

misconceptions.question: Why does a more concentrated solution react faster?
misconceptions.correct: There are more particles in the same volume, so collisions are more frequent.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles in a concentrated solution move faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Stronger' and 'more concentrated' get mixed with 'hotter', and faster particles are the explanation used for temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions. Particle speed depends on temperature, not concentration.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the concentration, pressure or surface area change the activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: No: it changes how often particles collide, not the energy they need.
misconceptions.misconception: These changes lower the activation energy of the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Activation energy is the phrase most firmly attached to rate, so it is offered as the explanation for every change that speeds a reaction up.
misconceptions.correction: Only a catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy. The other factors work by changing collision frequency, or frequency and energy for temperature.

misconceptions.question: Why does magnesium powder react faster than a strip of the same mass?
misconceptions.correct: The powder has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent.
misconceptions.misconception: There is more magnesium in the powder than in the strip.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The powder looks like more material because it spreads out, and equal masses are not compared.
misconceptions.correction: The masses are the same. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area to volume ratio, exposing more particles to collide.

misconceptions.question: Give the full reason why heating speeds a reaction up.
misconceptions.correct: Collisions become more frequent and a greater proportion of them are energetic enough to react.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating only makes the particles collide more often.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The collision-frequency explanation works for concentration and pressure, so it is reused for temperature and the energy half is left out.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.

misconceptions.question: Why does raising the pressure of reacting gases speed the reaction up?
misconceptions.correct: The same particles occupy a smaller volume, so they collide more often.
misconceptions.misconception: Squeezing the gas makes each collision more energetic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is felt as a force pushing particles together, and a harder push sounds like a harder collision.
misconceptions.correction: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions. The energy of the collisions depends on temperature.

misconceptions.question: Doubling the concentration roughly doubles the rate. What does halving it do?
misconceptions.correct: It roughly halves the rate, because the collision frequency roughly halves.
misconceptions.misconception: It cuts the rate to a quarter, because rate depends on concentration squared.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Proportional' is confused with a squared relationship, or the halving is applied twice.
misconceptions.correction: Simple proportionality is what the specification asks for: half the particles in the same volume gives about half the collision frequency and about half the rate.

misconceptions.question: Is a catalyst used up during a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No: catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is slowly used up and has to be replaced.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything else added to a reaction mixture gets consumed, so a catalyst is assumed to behave the same way.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst can be recovered at the end and is not included in the chemical equation for the reaction.

misconceptions.question: Will one good catalyst speed up any reaction?
misconceptions.correct: No: different reactions need different catalysts.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst is a general speeding-up substance that works on any reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word catalyst is used loosely outside chemistry to mean anything that makes something happen faster.
misconceptions.correction: Different reactions need different catalysts, and enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.

misconceptions.question: Does adding a catalyst increase the amount of product a reaction makes?
misconceptions.correct: No: it changes the rate, so the same product is made sooner.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst makes the reaction produce more product than it would otherwise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Faster and more are both improvements, so they are treated as the same improvement.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst changes the rate of the reaction. The reactants and products, and their energies on a reaction profile, are unchanged.

misconceptions.question: How does a catalyst lower the activation energy?
misconceptions.correct: It provides a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.
misconceptions.misconception: It lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Lowers the activation energy' is the half of the sentence that gets remembered, and the different pathway is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.

misconceptions.question: On a reaction profile, what does a catalyst change?
misconceptions.correct: Only the height of the hump: the reactants and products stay at the same energies.
misconceptions.misconception: The catalyst also lowers the energy level of the products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One lowered feature on the diagram is generalised to the whole curve being pulled down.
misconceptions.correction: A reaction profile for a catalysed reaction is drawn with a lower activation energy hump, while the reactant and product energies are unchanged.

misconceptions.question: A solid speeds a reaction up but does not appear in the equation. What is it?
misconceptions.correct: A catalyst: it is identified by its effect on the rate and its absence from the equation.
misconceptions.misconception: A substance in the flask must be a reactant if added at the start, or a product if present at the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything put into the flask at the beginning is assumed to be a reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to identify catalysts in reactions from their effect on the rate of reaction and because they are not included in the chemical equation.

misconceptions.question: Are enzymes catalysts?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
misconceptions.misconception: Any solid substance that speeds up a reaction must be an enzyme.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Enzymes are met in biology and catalysts in chemistry, so the two are filed separately.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems, speeding reactions up without being used up.

misconceptions.question: Is stirring one of the factors the specification lists as affecting rate?
misconceptions.correct: No: the listed factors are concentration, pressure of reacting gases, surface area, temperature and catalysts.
misconceptions.misconception: Stirring the mixture, and the colour of the reactants, are factors that change the rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Stirring is something students always do in the laboratory and it does help mix reactants, so it is remembered as one of the taught factors; colour is confused with the colour change used to follow some reactions.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists the concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.

misconceptions.question: A reaction is timed in seconds. Can the rate be quoted per minute?
misconceptions.correct: Not in an answer that asks for the rate in cm³ /s: the time unit must match the one used.
misconceptions.misconception: The value worked out from readings in seconds can be written with /min on the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Practical work is often described in minutes while the readings are taken in seconds, so the two time units are swapped without converting.
misconceptions.correction: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s. Changing the time unit changes the number as well, so the value and the unit must agree.

mcqs.stem: A student follows the reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, which gives off carbon dioxide. Which set of measurements would allow the mean rate of reaction to be worked out?

options.text: The volume of gas collected, together with the time taken to collect it
options.rationale: The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of product formed over time, so a quantity and a time are both needed.

options.text: The total volume of gas given off at the end, and nothing else
options.rationale: A quantity on its own answers 'how much', not 'how fast'; with no time there is nothing to divide by.

options.text: The time taken until the fizzing finally stops, and nothing more
options.rationale: The stopwatch reading feels like the answer, but time is only the denominator of the calculation.

options.text: The temperature of the mixture, measured every ten seconds
options.rationale: Recorded over time, so it has the right shape, but temperature is not a quantity of reactant or product.

mcqs.stem: In a reaction, 3.6 g of magnesium ribbon is used up in 180 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.020 g/min
options.rationale: Correct per-second value wrongly written with /min — the seconds-to-minutes label slip (m37).
mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken) = 3.6 g / 180 s.

options.text: 50 g/s
options.rationale: 180 divided by 3.6: the division is done the wrong way round, giving time per gram.
3.6 multiplied by 180, chosen by students who multiply rather than divide.

mcqs.stem: A gas syringe collects 12 cm³ of gas in 8 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.67 cm³ /s
options.rationale: 8 divided by 12, which inverts the calculation and gives time per cm³ .

options.text: 1.5 cm³ /min
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right but the time unit does not match the seconds that were measured.

options.text: 1.5 cm³ /s
options.rationale: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken) = 12 cm³ / 8 s.

options.text: 96 cm³ /s
options.rationale: 12 multiplied by 8, chosen by students who multiply rather than divide.

mcqs.stem: The specification states how the quantity of a reactant or product may be measured. Which pair does it give?

options.text: The concentration in mol/dm³ or the temperature in °C
options.rationale: These are the numbers most often written on the bottles, but neither is a quantity of substance.

options.text: The mass in grams or the total time taken in seconds
options.rationale: Time is the other measurement a rate needs, not a way of measuring the quantity.

options.text: The volume in cm³ or the pressure of the gas in pascals
options.rationale: Pressure is a condition that affects the rate, not a measure of how much gas has formed.

options.text: The mass measured in grams or the volume in cm³
options.rationale: The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ .

mcqs.stem: Which of these is given in the specification as a unit of rate of reaction?

options.text: s/cm³
options.rationale: The quantity and the time have been written the wrong way round.

options.text: cm³ /s
options.rationale: The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s.

options.text: mol/dm³
options.rationale: Confuses rate with concentration, giving mol/dm³ (m05).

options.text: cm³
options.rationale: This is the unit of the volume measured, with no time in it at all.

mcqs.stem: (HT) In a Higher Tier question the quantity of a reactant is given in moles. In which unit should the rate of reaction then be given?

options.text: mol/dm³
options.rationale: mol/dm³ is a concentration, the unit met most often alongside moles.

options.text: s /mol
options.rationale: Writes the rate unit upside-down, time on top (m06).

options.text: mol
options.rationale: This is the unit of the quantity itself, with the per-second part missing.

options.text: mol/s
options.rationale: For the Higher Tier, units for rate of reaction may be given in mol/s.

mcqs.stem: (HT) In a reaction, 0.60 mol of hydrogen is produced in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 0.020 mol/min
options.rationale: Correct 0.020 value mislabelled per minute instead of per second (m37).
The number is right but the unit given is that of the quantity, not the rate.

options.text: 0.020 mol/s
options.rationale: 0.60 mol divided by 30 s, with the rate given in mol/s as the Higher Tier requires.

options.text: 18 mol/s
options.rationale: 0.60 multiplied by 30, from multiplying rather than dividing.

mcqs.stem: A flask of reacting mixture stands on a balance. The mass falls from 82.50 g to 81.90 g in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?

options.rationale: Correct 0.0050 value mislabelled per minute (m37).
The mass lost is reported as the rate, with the division by time left out.
The mass lost is 0.60 g, and 0.60 g divided by 120 s gives 0.0050 g/s.
120 divided by 0.60, which turns the calculation upside down.

mcqs.stem: Experiment X produces 30 cm³ of gas in 20 s. Experiment Y produces 45 cm³ of gas in 45 s. Which statement about the mean rates is correct?

options.text: Y is faster, because Y produces the larger total volume of gas
options.rationale: The larger volume is compared without dividing by the time taken.

options.text: Y is faster, because the reaction in Y was allowed to run for longer
options.rationale: A longer time gives a smaller rate for a given quantity, not a larger one.

options.text: The mean rates are equal, since both experiments make gas steadily
options.rationale: Steady production does not make two different rates equal; 1.5 and 1.0 differ.

options.text: X is faster: its mean rate is 1.5 cm³ /s and the mean rate of Y is 1.0 cm³ /s
options.rationale: Each quantity is divided by its own time before the two are compared.

mcqs.stem: A graph of the volume of gas produced against time is steep at first and then becomes less steep. What does this shape show?

options.text: The volume of gas begins to fall once the curve bends over
options.rationale: 'Levelling off' is read as 'going down', but the line still rises.

options.text: The reaction speeds up steadily as more product forms
options.rationale: This would give a curve that becomes steeper, not less steep.

options.text: The reaction runs at one steady rate the whole way
options.rationale: A constant rate would give a straight line, not a curve.

options.text: The reaction is fastest at the start, and then slows down
options.rationale: Steepness of the curve is a measure of rate, so a falling steepness means a falling rate.

mcqs.stem: The line on a graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal after 80 s. What does this tell you?

options.text: No more gas is being made, so the reaction has ended
options.rationale: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the rate is zero and the reaction has stopped.

options.text: Gas is now being made at a steady, constant rate
options.rationale: A straight line is remembered as a constant rate without checking that its slope is zero.

options.text: The reaction is still speeding up, but more gradually
options.rationale: A speeding-up reaction gives a curve that steepens, not a flat line.

options.text: The gas is now being used up again in a reverse reaction
options.rationale: That would make the volume fall; the line is level, not falling.

mcqs.stem: A student needs the rate of reaction at 30 s from a curved graph of volume of gas against time. What should the student do?

options.text: Draw a tangent at 30 s and work out its slope
options.rationale: The specification requires a tangent to be drawn and its slope used as a measure of the rate.

options.text: Read the volume off the curve at 30 s and use that
options.rationale: The height of the curve is the quantity made so far, not the rate.

options.text: Join the origin to the point at 30 s and use that slope
options.rationale: That gives the mean rate over the first 30 s, not the rate at 30 s.

options.text: Divide the final volume by the total time of the run
options.rationale: This is the mean rate for the whole reaction, not the rate at one moment.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A tangent drawn to a volume-time curve at 20 s passes through the points (10 s, 12 cm³ ) and (30 s, 52 cm³ ). What is the rate of reaction at 20 s?

options.text: 2.0 cm³ /s
options.rationale: The gradient is (52 - 12) cm³ divided by (30 - 10) s = 40 / 20 = 2.0 cm³ /s.

options.text: 0.50 cm³ /s
options.rationale: 20 divided by 40, which inverts the gradient.

options.text: 40 cm³ /s
options.rationale: Only the rise is used; the run of 20 s is never divided in.

options.text: 2.0 cm³
options.rationale: The gradient is right but the unit has no time in it.

mcqs.stem: Which list contains only factors that the specification says affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, time
options.rationale: Time changes how much product has formed, not how fast it forms.

options.text: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, catalysts
options.rationale: This is exactly the list the specification gives.

options.text: Concentration, colour of the reactants, temperature, stirring, catalysts
options.rationale: Stirring helps mixing and colour is used to follow some reactions, but neither is on the specification's list.

options.text: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, pH, volume of flask
options.rationale: The volume of the flask does not change the rate, and pH is not one of the factors.

mcqs.stem: A reaction mixture is cooled from 40 °C to 20 °C. What happens to the rate of the reaction?

options.text: It increases, because cooling packs the particles closer together
options.rationale: Cooling a solution barely changes how closely packed it is, and the particles move more slowly.

options.text: It decreases, as collisions are less frequent and less energetic
options.rationale: Students should be able to recall that lowering the temperature lowers the rate.

options.text: It is unchanged, since temperature affects only the final amount made
options.rationale: Temperature is one of the listed factors that affects the rate itself.

options.text: It decreases, but only if a catalyst is taken out as well
options.rationale: Cooling lowers the rate whether or not a catalyst is present.

mcqs.stem: Required practical 5 investigates how changes in concentration affect the rate of reaction. Which pair of methods does the specification require?

options.text: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following the temperature rise in the flask
options.rationale: A temperature rise is assumed to belong in every rate experiment, but it is not one of the two methods.

options.text: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following a colour change or turbidity
options.rationale: These are the two methods named in Required practical 5.

options.text: Measuring the temperature rise, and following a colour change or turbidity
options.rationale: Wrongly treats a temperature measurement as a way to track rate (m19).

options.text: Weighing the solid left behind, and following the volume of the solution used
options.rationale: Neither is a method the practical uses to follow the change in concentration.

mcqs.stem: Required practical 5 should involve developing a hypothesis. Which of these is a suitable hypothesis for the investigation?

options.text: The higher the concentration of the acid, the faster gas will be produced
options.rationale: It is a testable prediction linking the independent variable to the dependent variable.

options.text: Measure the volume of gas every ten seconds for each concentration used
options.rationale: This is the method: what will be done, not what is predicted.

options.text: Add the acid to the magnesium and time each reaction with a stopwatch
options.rationale: Gives an experimental procedure, mistaking it for a hypothesis (m20).

options.text: Concentration and rate of reaction are connected in some way
options.rationale: Too vague to test: it makes no prediction that the results could contradict.

mcqs.stem: According to collision theory, when can a reaction between two particles take place?

options.text: Whenever they collide, no matter how gently they hit each other
options.rationale: 'Particles must collide' is remembered but the energy condition is dropped.

options.text: Only when the collision itself gives out enough energy
options.rationale: Thinks a reaction needs the collision to release enough energy (m22).

options.text: Only when they collide with at least the activation energy
options.rationale: Reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.

options.text: Whenever they are in the same container as each other
options.rationale: Being mixed is not enough; a collision with sufficient energy is needed.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: The energy given out as the products are formed
options.rationale: Defines activation energy as the energy released forming products (m22).

options.text: The energy that is given out when the particles collide and react
options.rationale: Energy changes are usually met as energy released, so any energy is assumed to be an output.

options.text: The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of activation energy.

options.text: The total energy needed to make all the particles react
options.rationale: Activation energy is a minimum per collision, not a total for the whole mixture.

mcqs.stem: Why does increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?

options.text: The acid particles move faster, so their collisions carry more energy
options.rationale: Particle speed depends on temperature, not on how concentrated the solution is.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra acid
options.rationale: Only a catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy.

options.text: More particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions
options.rationale: Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions.

options.text: Each single collision becomes much more likely to end in a reaction
options.rationale: The proportion of successful collisions is unchanged; there are simply more of them.

mcqs.stem: A 5 g strip of magnesium and 5 g of magnesium powder are added to separate beakers of the same acid. Why does the powder react faster?

options.text: There is simply more magnesium in the powder than in the strip
options.rationale: The two masses are equal; the powder only looks like more.

options.text: It has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent
options.rationale: The effect of the size of the pieces is explained in terms of surface area to volume ratio.

options.text: The powder particles move faster, so the collisions are more energetic
options.rationale: Grinding a solid does not change how fast its particles move.

options.text: The powder must lower the activation energy needed by the reaction
options.rationale: Surface area changes collision frequency, not the energy barrier.

mcqs.stem: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction? Give the full reason.

options.text: Collisions are more frequent, and that is the whole of the reason why
options.rationale: The frequency explanation is reused from concentration and the energy half is left out.

options.text: Collisions happen more often, and nothing else about them changes
options.rationale: Thinks heating only makes collisions more frequent, nothing else (m26).

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction falls as it is heated
options.rationale: Heating changes the particles, not the energy barrier of the reaction.

options.text: Collisions are more frequent and more of them are energetic enough
options.rationale: Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic.

mcqs.stem: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure of the gases increase the rate of reaction?

options.text: Squeezing the particles closer together makes each collision harder
options.rationale: Pressure feels like a push, but the energy of collisions depends on temperature.

options.text: Raising the pressure lowers the energy that a successful collision needs
options.rationale: The activation energy is fixed unless a catalyst provides a new pathway.

options.text: There are more gas particles present than there were before
options.rationale: No gas is added; the same particles are confined to a smaller space.

options.text: The particles are in a smaller volume, so they collide more often
options.rationale: Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions.

mcqs.stem: Doubling the concentration of a solution roughly doubles the rate of reaction. Using simple ideas about proportionality, what should halving the concentration do?

options.text: Cut the rate to a quarter, since the rate depends on the square
options.rationale: A squared relationship is assumed where simple proportionality applies.

options.text: Cut the rate by more than half, as the particles also move slower
options.rationale: Thinks diluting also slows particles, cutting rate more than half (m23).

options.text: Leave the rate unchanged, since the same amount of acid still reacts
options.rationale: The final amount may be smaller, but it is the rate that is being asked about.

options.text: Roughly halve the rate, as collisions become half as frequent
options.rationale: Simple proportionality: half the particles in the same volume gives about half the collision frequency.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about catalysts is correct?

options.text: A catalyst is used up slowly, so more must be added as it goes
options.rationale: Everything else added to a mixture is consumed, so a catalyst is assumed to be too.

options.text: One catalyst will speed up any reaction that it is added to
options.rationale: Different reactions need different catalysts.

options.text: A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction but is not used up by it
options.rationale: Catalysts change the rate of chemical reactions but are not used up during the reaction.

options.text: A catalyst makes a reaction produce more of the product
options.rationale: Faster and larger yield are treated as the same improvement, but only the rate changes.

mcqs.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?

options.text: It provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy
options.rationale: This is the specification's explanation of catalytic action.

options.text: It lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway
options.rationale: Half the sentence is remembered; the different pathway is the part that is dropped.

options.text: It speeds up any reaction at all, as catalysts always do
options.rationale: Treats a catalyst as a general speeder of any reaction (m30).

options.text: It makes the reaction produce more product, so it goes faster
options.rationale: Thinks a catalyst makes more product, so assumes it is faster (m31).

mcqs.stem: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, how does the catalysed curve differ from the uncatalysed one?

options.text: Its hump is lower, and the reactants and products are unchanged
options.rationale: The lower hump shows the lower activation energy of the new pathway; the energy levels stay the same.

options.text: Its hump is lower, and the products end up at a lower energy too
options.rationale: One lowered feature is generalised to the whole diagram being pulled down.

options.text: Its hump is lower, and it makes more product as well
options.rationale: Correct lower hump, but wrongly adds extra product (m31).

options.text: The hump is the same, but the curve reaches products sooner
options.rationale: A reaction profile plots energy, not time, so 'sooner' cannot be shown on it.

mcqs.stem: The equation for a reaction is 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. A solid is added to the flask, the reaction speeds up, and the solid is recovered unchanged at the end. What is the solid?

options.text: A reactant, because it was added to the flask before the reaction started
options.rationale: Anything put in at the start is assumed to be a reactant, but reactants appear in the equation.

options.text: A catalyst, as it speeds the reaction up and is not in the equation
options.rationale: Catalysts are identified from their effect on the rate and from their absence from the chemical equation.

options.text: A product, because it was there in the flask at the end of the reaction
options.rationale: It was there at the start as well, and products appear in the equation.

options.text: An enzyme, because it is a solid substance that speeds the reaction up
options.rationale: Enzymes are the catalysts of biological systems; nothing here says this solid is biological.
